title: Verb tense, irregular verbs and consistency
blurb: Keep tenses consistent, use the perfect tenses for the right timing, and get irregular forms and lie/lay right every time.
question: A shift note reads, “At 8 a.m., Mr. Diaz complains of back pain. He had laid in bed all night and has drank only one glass of water.” Which verbs are wrong, and what should they be?

teach.body: Formally, tense is the form of a verb that shows the time of an action: past, present or future, each with simple and perfect forms. Plain English: the verb is the clock in the sentence. Readers trust that clock, so it must not jump from past to present without a reason, and each verb must use its correct form. The TEAS tests three things: consistent tense, the right perfect tense, and correct irregular forms.

teach.caption: “She had left before the doctor arrived”: had left happened first, so it takes the past perfect.

teach.h: Simple past vs the perfect tenses
Do not shift tense without a reason
teach.body: Pick a time frame and stay in it. “Jo opens the file and read the notes” jumps from present to past for no reason: make both opened and read, or both opens and reads. A shift is correct only when the time really changes: “Last year Omar volunteered at a clinic; now he works there.” In a paragraph, check every verb against the time frame of its neighbors.

head: Base
Past
Past participle
teach.caption: The past participle is the form used after has, have or had (and after is/was in the passive).

rows.label: I have saw the new schedule.
I have seen the new schedule.

teach.note: Past forms stand alone; past participles need has, have or had. Could of, should of and would of are always wrong.

teach.caption: Same pattern: sit (no object) vs set (set something); rise (no object, rose, risen) vs raise (raise something, raised).

teach.h: Scenario: Priya corrects a shift note
teach.body: CNA and nursing applicant Priya Shah reviews: “At 8 a.m., Mr. Diaz complains of back pain. He had laid in bed all night and has drank only one glass of water.” Fix 1: the note describes the past, so complains becomes complained. Fix 2: lying in bed takes no object, so the past participle of lie is needed: had lain. Fix 3: drank is the simple past; after a helping verb use the participle, and the earlier action needs the past perfect: had drunk.

teach.text: Lay is BOTH the present of lay and the past of lie. “Yesterday I lay down” is correct; “Yesterday I laid down” is wrong because nothing was put down. If you can add “something” after the verb, use lay/laid; if not, use lie/lay/lain.

items: Stay in one time frame; shift tense only when the time actually changes.
Present perfect (has worked) links past to now; past perfect (had worked) marks the earlier of two past events.
Past participles (seen, gone, drunk, written) need has, have or had; past forms (saw, went, drank) stand alone.
Never could of, should of or would of: use could have, should have, would have.
Lie/lay/lain (recline, no object) vs lay/laid/laid (put something down); sit vs set; rise vs raise.
Subjunctive (low weight): “If I were you,” “The doctor recommends that she take ...”

summary: You can now keep verb tenses consistent, choose the present or past perfect when the timing calls for it, and use the correct past and past participle forms of irregular verbs. You can also separate lie from lay, sit from set and rise from raise.

A.q: Which verb correctly completes the sentence? “By the time the doctor arrived, the patient had ___ two glasses of water.”
A.why: After had, use the past participle. The forms are drink, drank, drunk, so had drunk.

whyNot.0: Drank is the simple past and cannot follow had.
whyNot.2: Drinked is not a standard form; drink is irregular.
whyNot.3: Drink is the base form and cannot follow had.

A.q: Which sentence uses the verb form correctly?
options: I seen the updated policy on the staff board.
She has went to the pharmacy for the new refill.
We should of asked the pharmacist before noon.
They have written their essays for the program.
A.why: Have needs the past participle, and written is the past participle of write.

whyNot.0: Seen is a past participle and needs a helping verb: I saw or I have seen.
whyNot.1: After has, the participle gone is needed: she has gone.
whyNot.2: Should of is a mishearing of should have.

A.q: Which sentence keeps the verb tense consistent?
options: Ana checks the vitals and recorded them in the chart.
Ana checked the vitals and records them in the chart.
Ana checked the vitals and recorded them in the chart.
Ana checks the vitals and had recorded them in the chart.
A.why: Both verbs are in the simple past, describing two actions in the same time frame.

whyNot.0: Shifts from present (checks) to past (recorded) with no change in time.
whyNot.1: Shifts from past (checked) to present (records) with no change in time.
whyNot.3: Had recorded says the recording came before the checking, which is illogical, and it clashes with the present checks.

B.q: Which verb correctly completes the sentence? “After the long shift, Jamal ___ down on the couch and slept for an hour.”
B.why: Jamal reclined (no object), so the verb is lie. Its past tense is lay, matching the past slept.

whyNot.1: Laid is the past of lay (to put something down) and needs an object.
whyNot.2: Lied is the past of lie meaning to tell an untruth.
whyNot.3: Layed is a misspelling; the past of lay is laid.

B.q: Which sentence correctly shows that the nurse's leaving came before the doctor's arrival?
options: The nurse has left before the doctor arrived.
The nurse had left before the doctor arrived.
The nurse leaves before the doctor arrived.
The nurse had leaved before the doctor arrived.
B.why: The past perfect had left marks the earlier of two past actions.

whyNot.0: Present perfect (has left) cannot be paired with a finished past moment like arrived.
whyNot.2: Shifts from present (leaves) to past (arrived) without reason.
whyNot.3: Leave is irregular: its past participle is left, not leaved.

B.q: Which sentence about the patient's chart is correct?
options: She lay the chart on the counter before rounds.
She laid down for a nap before her night shift.
She has lain the chart on the counter already today.
She laid the chart on the counter before rounds.
B.why: Putting the chart down takes an object, so the verb is lay; its past is laid.

whyNot.0: Lay is present tense here and would need lays for she; the past is laid.
whyNot.1: Napping takes no object, so the past of lie is needed: she lay down.
whyNot.2: Lain is the participle of lie (recline); with an object, use has laid.

C.q: Read the paragraph. (1) Last spring, Keisha volunteered at a free clinic. (2) She greeted patients and filled out intake forms. (3) Each week she learns more about patient care. (4) By June, she had decided to apply to nursing school. Which sentence contains an unnecessary tense shift?
C.why: The paragraph narrates last spring in the past tense. Sentence 3 jumps to the present (learns) for no reason; it should be learned.

whyNot.0: Volunteered is simple past, matching “Last spring.”
whyNot.1: Greeted and filled are simple past, consistent with the paragraph.
whyNot.3: Had decided is correct past perfect: the decision was complete by June.

C.q: Which sentence uses the correct past participle?
options: The pipes had froze overnight, so the clinic opened late.
The lab tech has broken two slides since Monday morning.
The bell had rang twice before the exam began on time.
The students had swam laps before their morning class.
C.why: Break, broke, broken: has needs the past participle broken.

whyNot.0: Freeze, froze, frozen: had needs frozen.
whyNot.2: Ring, rang, rung: had needs rung.
whyNot.3: Swim, swam, swum: had needs swum.

C.q: Which sentence uses the verb correctly?
options: Please raise the head of the bed before meals.
The patient tried to raise from the chair slowly.
Please set down in the waiting room until called.
Clinic fees have raised sharply since last year.
C.why: Raise takes an object (the head of the bed), so raise is correct.

whyNot.1: Getting up takes no object, so the verb is rise: tried to rise.
whyNot.2: Taking a seat takes no object, so the verb is sit: please sit down.
whyNot.3: Fees going up takes no object, so the verb is rise: have risen.

reteach.title: The verb is the clock on the wall
reteach.question: Imagine a story read aloud while a clock on the wall shows the time. What happens if the clock keeps jumping between yesterday and today?

blocks.body: A story set yesterday keeps the clock on yesterday: walked, asked, wrote. If one sentence suddenly says writes, the listener thinks the clock jumped to today. The only reason to move the clock is a real change in time, and the perfect tenses are how you show those moves: had marks something even earlier than yesterday, and has stretches from the past right up to now.

blocks.text: Irregular verbs break the clock's pattern: there is no “drinked,” “swimmed” or “leaved.” Learn the three forms (drink, drank, drunk) as a set.

explain.body: Verbs describing the same time frame use the same tense. Change tense only when the time actually changes.

test.q: Which pair of verbs removes the tense shift in “The patient walks to the desk and asked for water”?
test.why: Both actions happen in the same past moment, so both verbs take the simple past: walked and asked.

whyNot.1: Still shifts from present to past perfect, which would put the asking before the walking.
whyNot.2: Simply reverses the shift: past then present.
whyNot.3: Walking is not a complete verb, so the sentence would have no main verb for its first action.

explain.body: Present perfect (has/have + participle) covers action that began in the past and continues or still matters now. Past perfect (had + participle) marks the earlier of two past actions.

test.q: Which verb correctly completes the sentence? “Kevin ___ as a CNA for three years and still works at the same nursing home.”
test.why: The work began in the past and continues now (still works), which is the present perfect: has worked.

whyNot.0: Had worked suggests the work ended before another past event, but he still works there.
whyNot.1: Simple present cannot carry “for three years” of past-to-present time.
whyNot.3: Future perfect looks ahead to a future point, which the sentence does not mention.

explain.body: Irregular verbs change their spelling instead of adding -ed. The past form stands alone; the past participle follows has, have or had.

test.q: Which word correctly completes the sentence? “The committee has ___ six applicants for interviews next week.”
test.why: After has, use the past participle. Choose, chose, chosen: has chosen.

whyNot.0: Chose is the simple past and cannot follow has.
whyNot.1: Choosed is not a standard form; choose is irregular.
whyNot.2: Choose is the base form and cannot follow has.

explain.body: Lie, sit and rise take no object. Lay, set and raise act on something. Ask: can I add “something” after the verb?

test.q: Which verb correctly completes the sentence? “Every afternoon, the patient ___ down for an hour after lunch.”
test.why: The patient reclines (no object), and the habit is in the present: lies.

whyNot.1: Lays means puts something down and needs an object.
whyNot.2: Laid is the past of lay and needs an object; the sentence is also present tense.
whyNot.3: Lain is a past participle and needs has or had.
